articles.title: Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03754-0Studies are more likely to be cited in patents if they are freely available — legitimately or otherwise — researchers have found.
articles.content:
Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty

Open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere. Industries that rely heavily on scientific discoveries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, disproportionately cite open-access work in their patents over paywalled research, a study has found.

An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.

When the study authors expanded the definition of open access to include papers available on Sci-Hub, a website that hosts pirated copies of scientific articles, this over-representation was even stronger. Papers that were freely available (either through the journal publishers or Sci-Hub) were 3.41 times more prevalent in patent citations than they were in the wider scientific literature.

The findings, published in Scientometrics, show how heavily inventors lean on open-access research, says study co-author Abdelghani Maddi, a scientometrics researcher at Sorbonne University in Paris. When you include platforms such as Sci-Hub, “the numbers are striking”, he says. “Open science is not only about who can read science, it’s about who can build on it.”

Open for innovation

For their analysis, Maddi and his colleagues leveraged the ‘Reliance on Science’ data set, a publicly available tool that identifies citation links between patents and journal publications2. They found that research-intensive industries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, cite the scientific literature (both open and pay-walled) in their patents much more heavily than do more engineering-based industries, such as vehicle- and construction-equipment manufacturing.

The researchers also showed that patents from countries with a high proportion of high-tech industries, including South Korea, Singapore and Denmark, cite more scientific publications than do those from countries with more heavy manufacturing industries, such as South Africa, Brazil and Italy.

To track patent citations of open-access papers specifically, the team cross-referenced research publications in the Reliance on Science patent database against those in OpenAlex, an index that catalogues hundreds of millions of scientific documents. They then used a normalization metric to account for differences in open-access publishing practices across research disciplines. Open-access publishing is much more prevalent in the health sciences than it is in computer science, for example, says Maddi.

Seeing how open-access papers were over-represented in patent citations suggests that making research freely accessible does more than just help people to read and share scientific findings, says study co-author Francesco De Pretis, an applied mathematician at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia in Italy. It also makes that knowledge more likely to be used in developing new technologies and inventions, he adds. “Our findings show that open science is not just a matter for academia, it’s also the business of industry and of national economies.”

Easy access

Matt Marx, an innovation and entrepreneurship researcher at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, whose team developed the Reliance on Science database, says the finding that patents tend to cite open-access papers “is especially intriguing”. But he cautions against assuming that ease of access is the only factor at play. “Perhaps inventors are more likely to cite papers they can read because those are open access, or it could be that prominent or important papers are more likely to be open-source,” he says.

Regardless of the exact causes, the access barrier is real, says Marin Dacos, who heads the open-science taskforce in France’s Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space. Negotiating contracts with thousands of journal publishers worldwide requires specialist library staff — a resource that is generally only available to large companies and universities, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant positive impact of open-access publishing on innovation by showing that freely accessible research is cited more frequently in patents, which drives technological development and benefits industries and economies broadly. It provides detailed analysis and evidence, emphasizing the broad societal and economic benefits of open science.

articles.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
articles.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.
articles.content:
For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.

Recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. These unusual mammals persisted for roughly 20 million years.

However, new research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.

"Males have been interpreted as being much larger and possessing far more dramatic cranial features than females," said study author Kevin Mulcahy, doctoral student at the KU Biodiversity Institute & Natural History Museum.

A Broken Fossil Tooth Leads to an Unexpected Discovery

The investigation began when Mulcahy and his doctoral adviser, K. Christopher Beard, senior curator at the institute, attempted to identify a broken upper molar recovered during fieldwork in Montana. The researchers suspected the tooth belonged to a uintathere but needed additional fossil specimens to confirm its identity.

"We had a research visit at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, where our main goal was just to compare that tooth to teeth from other uintatheres and figure out what type of animal we had," Mulcahy said. "They have this big collection -- entire shelves occupied with these skulls, and each one of them is almost a meter long. These are famous specimens that are in the literature, and I was originally just looking at them to compare their teeth, and I noticed a ton of variation in a way that didn't appear binary."

Intrigued by the unexpected range of physical characteristics, Mulcahy began measuring the skulls in the museum's collection.

"I just, really hastily, with a ruler, gathered a bunch of measurements of the skulls while we were there," Mulcahy said. "I started playing around with statistics, and there are ways you can look at different measurements to see if they're best fit by a classic unimodal distribution, or if you were to think you're dealing with something that exhibits strong sexual dimorphism, you'd see something with a bimodal distribution -- that there are two means, one for males and one for females."

Ancient Skulls Challenge a Classic Example of Sexual Dimorphism

If males and females differed as dramatically as paleontologists had suggested, the skull measurements would be expected to cluster into two relatively distinct groups. Instead, Mulcahy's initial analysis failed to reveal such a clear separation.

"It wasn't like there's one group of specimens that look bigger than another, and then there's another group that are smaller with smaller horns and canines," he said. "So I was kind of interested -- are these really good examples of sexual dimorphism after all? Is there actual evidence in the morphology of these skulls, in the distribution in particular of the ranges of morphology we're seeing, that that's what's going on?"

To investigate further, Mulcahy collected additional measurements from fossils housed at other institutions and expanded his analysis using new statistical methods. His final dataset encompassed approximately 30 skulls belonging to a single extinct species, Uintatherium anceps.

Although the results offered some hints of physical differences between the sexes, the evidence was far less convincing than expected. One major challenge in studying extinct animals is that researchers generally cannot independently determine the sex of individual fossil specimens.

"Maybe there were some little signals of dimorphism here and there, but nothing really concrete," he said. "I had an idea: Maybe it's just that the techniques I'm using aren't robust enough to actually measure sexual dimorphism. With fossil animals, you don't actually know which specimens are males and which are females. You can guess and then test whether or not the ones you guess are males differ from the ones you guess are females, but that's super circular, because you could just be picking the most extreme ones to be one sex and the least extreme to be the other. Of course they're going to differ."

Modern Bison Provide an Important Comparison

To determine whether his statistical methods could reliably detect sexual dimorphism, Mulcahy turned to a living mammal: the bison. Unlike fossil uintatheres, modern bison specimens could be classified by sex with confidence.

Bison also offered a useful comparison because they are large, horned herbivores whose ecology shares similarities with what researchers have proposed for uintatheres.

"When you're dealing with living animals, you can just take the males, take the females and compare them," he said. "Bison are another really big herbivore, with a similar sort of ecology that's been proposed for uintatheres, and they also have big horns. What I noticed is that the signals of dimorphism I was picking up in bison were a lot clearer. When I was looking at the bison, it was almost perfect that all of the females were most similar to the females, and all the males were most similar to the males."

The contrast suggests that the relatively weak evidence for sexual dimorphism in uintatheres cannot be attributed solely to limitations of the statistical techniques. The same methods successfully identified much clearer physical differences between male and female bison.

Victorian-Era Bias May Have Shaped Paleontology

Mulcahy believes that historical cultural attitudes may help explain why paleontologists came to accept such pronounced differences between male and female uintatheres. Many extinct species were first identified and described during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when prevailing views about the sexes may have influenced scientific interpretations.

"Back then, this is right when evolutionary theory, sexual selection, natural selection, all of that is kind of coming into play," he said. "I think it's really important to remember that these things were first discovered in the late 1800s by a bunch of male paleontologists working in a very Victorian-era mindset. The idea is basically assumed at that point that males are going to be bigger and scarier than females. It's really interesting: When you step back and actually test that hypothesis, it doesn't really hold up."

Because uintatheres have long been regarded as one of the clearest examples of sexual dimorphism in the fossil record, the new findings could have implications beyond these unusual prehistoric giants. Other extinct species may also have exhibited less pronounced physical differences between males and females than scientists have traditionally believed.

Rethinking the Evolution of Sex Differences in Mammals

The research also adds to a growing body of evidence challenging the widespread assumption that male mammals are typically larger than females. Dramatic differences in body size and physical appearance may have evolved independently in multiple mammalian lineages rather than being a characteristic inherited from their earliest common ancestors.

Research on living mammals has similarly challenged conventional thinking, suggesting that pronounced differences favoring larger males are less widespread than historically assumed.

"Strong, big male-style sexual dimorphism was probably not ancestral at the root of the mammalian tree, and among the mammals where we do see this pattern today, it's almost certainly shown up independently several times," Mulcahy said. "It had long been assumed that sexual dimorphism is the norm, that most species show that males are bigger than females. But just a couple years ago, a paper came out showing that among living mammals, most species either don't show any dimorphism or actually have larger females. The idea that males are always bigger than females is really just a choice of what animals were people looking at, what are the things that biologists in the past were interested in."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that challenges long-held assumptions about sexual dimorphism in prehistoric mammals, which has broad implications for paleontology and evolutionary biology. It provides detailed context and methodology, highlighting a breakthrough in understanding extinct species and correcting historical biases, thus advancing scientific knowledge.

**What happened** – A team from the University of Kansas studied broken teeth and skulls of uintatheres from museums. They measured about 30 skulls and used statistics to see if males and females really looked very different. Their results showed the differences were much smaller than previously thought.

**Impact** – This is important because uintatheres were a classic example used to explain sexual dimorphism, where males and females look very different. **What's next step** – Scientists will likely re-examine other prehistoric animals to check for similar mistakes. This could change how we understand the evolution of male and female traits in mammals over millions of years.

articles.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
articles.summary: The Age of Alchemy has just won the Royal Society Trivedi Science Book prize. As the New Scientist Book Club reads it, author Kit Chapman makes a case for the transformative powers of urine
articles.content:
The Age of Alchemy has just won the Royal Society Trivedi Science Book prize. As the New Scientist Book Club reads it, author Kit Chapman makes a case for the transformative powers of urine

A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy

Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick?

For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history.

Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter

The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce.

Advertisement

If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet, money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world.

The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia, the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X, part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. In it, the recipe suggests using the “urine of a small child”, although today our understanding of the chemical reaction that creates the effect means we know water is a better alternative.

Fast-forward a thousand years, and the mass use of urine was commonplace around the world. It was still used for laundry and leatherwork, but was now also part of the burgeoning gunpowder industry. One of the key ingredients of this game-changing superweapon, the origins of which lie in Chinese herbal medicine, is saltpetre, or potassium nitrate. This was gathered from nitre beds, stinking manure heaps mixed with potash and mortar, all moistened with urine to claim the nitrates. This method, used from Europe to Japan, continued well into the 19th century; during the US Civil War, the Confederacy was using urine to keep its guns firing.

But perhaps urine’s greatest contribution came from alchemy. By the 17th century, just as the printing press and improvements in lenses and glassware had finally begun to usher in the scientific method, the old practices and beliefs that blended experiment, philosophy, religion and misunderstanding of the ancient world had their greatest triumph. In 1669, an alchemist in Hamburg, Hennig Brand, was searching for the philosopher’s stone using 1500 gallons of fermented urine he had collected in his basement. To Brand’s astonishment, the concentrated urine at the heart of his experiment began to glow. Brand kept his accomplishment secret for years, but unable to take the next step and turn metals into gold, he eventually sold the recipe to a friend and the discovery was shared with the world. Brand hadn’t performed a magic trick, but isolated phosphorus – the first chemical element to be discovered in modern times.

Today, urine still plays a critical role around the world, particularly in medicine, where it is a source of biomarkers used in diagnostic tests, and was even the original source of drugs such as human chorionic gonadotropin and follicle-stimulating hormone for fertility treatment. As Emperor Vespasian said almost 2000 years ago, money doesn’t stink – and nor do the benefits of the amber liquid we all produce every day.

Kit Chapman is the author of The Age of Alchemy, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

When you make a purchase via the links on this page, we receive a commission.

articles.personality_title: How urine helped shape science and civilization
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For a long time, people have searched for special substances that could change the world. One such search was for the “Philosopher’s Stone” in medieval Europe, a mythical object that alchemists believed could turn metals into gold. But an unexpected and ordinary substance—urine—played a big role in human history instead.

**What happened** – In his book "The Age of Alchemy," author Kit Chapman explains how urine influenced many important developments. Urine contains urea, which breaks down into ammonia, helping early humans tan leather. Leather was crucial for making clothes and tools across many cultures. Ancient Romans even taxed urine because it was used to clean clothes. Alchemists later used urine in experiments, and in 1669, Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus by boiling large amounts of urine. This was the first modern chemical element discovered. Urine also helped produce saltpetre, an ingredient in gunpowder, used worldwide for centuries.

**Impact** – Urine’s role in tanning leather, cleaning, making gunpowder, and discovering phosphorus shows how ordinary materials can lead to big changes in science and daily life. The discovery of phosphorus helped start modern chemistry. The use of urine in medicine continues today, such as in fertility treatments and diagnostic tests.

**What's next step** – Understanding the history of urine’s role in science encourages new ways to look at common materials for future discoveries. Scientists and historians can explore other overlooked substances that might have important uses. This story also invites more people to appreciate how science builds on many small, everyday things.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Urine, a simple and common substance, has played a surprising and important part in shaping science, technology, and civilization throughout history.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment l’urine a façonné la science et la civilisation
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Pendant longtemps, les gens ont cherché des substances spéciales capables de changer le monde. Une de ces recherches concernait la « pierre philosophale » au Moyen Âge, un objet mythique censé transformer les métaux en or. Mais une substance ordinaire et inattendue — l’urine — a joué un grand rôle dans l’histoire humaine.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans son livre « L’Âge de l’alchimie », l’auteur Kit Chapman explique comment l’urine a influencé de nombreux développements importants. L’urine contient de l’urée, qui se décompose en ammoniaque, aidant les premiers humains à tanner le cuir. Le cuir était essentiel pour fabriquer vêtements et outils dans de nombreuses cultures. Les Romains anciens taxaient même l’urine car elle servait à laver les vêtements. Plus tard, les alchimistes utilisaient l’urine dans leurs expériences, et en 1669, Hennig Brand a découvert le phosphore en faisant bouillir beaucoup d’urine. Ce fut le premier élément chimique moderne découvert. L’urine a aussi aidé à produire le salpêtre, un ingrédient de la poudre à canon, utilisée dans le monde entier pendant des siècles.

**Impact** – Le rôle de l’urine dans le tannage du cuir, le nettoyage, la fabrication de la poudre à canon et la découverte du phosphore montre comment des matériaux ordinaires peuvent provoquer de grands changements en science et dans la vie quotidienne. La découverte du phosphore a aidé à lancer la chimie moderne. Aujourd’hui, l’urine est toujours utilisée en médecine, notamment dans les traitements de fertilité et les tests diagnostiques.

**Prochaine étape** – Comprendre l’histoire de l’urine en science encourage à chercher de nouvelles façons d’utiliser des matériaux communs pour de futures découvertes. Les scientifiques et historiens peuvent explorer d’autres substances négligées qui pourraient avoir des usages importants. Cette histoire invite aussi plus de personnes à apprécier comment la science se construit à partir de petits éléments quotidiens.

**En une phrase** – L’urine, substance simple et commune, a joué un rôle surprenant et important dans la formation de la science, de la technologie et de la civilisation à travers l’histoire.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo la orina ayudó a moldear la ciencia y la civilización
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, la gente ha buscado sustancias especiales que puedan cambiar el mundo. Una de esas búsquedas fue la «piedra filosofal» en la Europa medieval, un objeto mítico que los alquimistas creían que podía convertir metales en oro. Pero una sustancia común e inesperada—la orina—jugó un papel importante en la historia humana.

**Qué pasó** – En su libro "La Edad de la Alquimia", el autor Kit Chapman explica cómo la orina influyó en muchos desarrollos importantes. La orina contiene urea, que se descompone en amoníaco, ayudando a los primeros humanos a curtir el cuero. El cuero fue esencial para hacer ropa y herramientas en muchas culturas. Los antiguos romanos incluso gravaron la orina porque se usaba para limpiar ropa. Más tarde, los alquimistas usaron la orina en sus experimentos, y en 1669, Hennig Brand descubrió el fósforo al hervir grandes cantidades de orina. Este fue el primer elemento químico moderno descubierto. La orina también ayudó a producir salitre, un ingrediente de la pólvora, usado en todo el mundo durante siglos.

**Impacto** – El papel de la orina en el curtido del cuero, la limpieza, la fabricación de pólvora y el descubrimiento del fósforo muestra cómo materiales ordinarios pueden provocar grandes cambios en la ciencia y la vida diaria. El descubrimiento del fósforo ayudó a iniciar la química moderna. Hoy, la orina sigue siendo importante en medicina, como en tratamientos de fertilidad y pruebas diagnósticas.

**Próximo paso** – Entender la historia del papel de la orina en la ciencia anima a buscar nuevas formas de usar materiales comunes para futuros descubrimientos. Científicos e historiadores pueden explorar otras sustancias pasadas por alto que podrían tener usos importantes. Esta historia también invita a más personas a valorar cómo la ciencia se construye a partir de cosas pequeñas y cotidianas.

**Una frase clave** – La orina, una sustancia simple y común, ha tenido un papel sorprendente e importante en la formación de la ciencia, la tecnología y la civilización a lo largo de la historia.

articles.title: The leading cities in the world for high-quality research in 2025
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03468-3A decade of data on the top-performing science cities in the Nature Index.
articles.content:
Urban climbers

Changes in cities’ ranks in the natural sciences are shown for 2016 to 2025, as measured by Share in the Nature Index. Beijing remained in first place, while five more Chinese cities entered the top ten during the period. Two US cities that were once in the top 10 have since fallen out of the top 20.

Source: Nature Index

Lifeline

The leading cities for biological sciences in 2025 are shown alongside their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. This is the most geographically diverse of the natural-sciences subjects, with four US, four Chinese and two European cities in the top 10.

Strong chemistry

Chinese cities take all top 10 places in the chemistry rankings for 2025, shown here with their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. Beijing and Shanghai had the highest growth over the period among the top 50 cities in the subject, each increasing their chemistry adjusted Share by almost 900.

Down to Earth

Beijing contributed 25% of China’s Earth and environmental sciences Share in 2025 — the highest percentage among the top-five cities in the natural-sciences and health-sciences subject areas. Among the top 10 cities in Earth and environmental sciences for 2025, Qingdao had the biggest percentage change in adjusted Share between 2016 and 2025, at 545.5%, and Beijing gained the most adjusted Share points, at 703.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights significant global progress and shifts in high-quality scientific research output across major cities, indicating broad advancements in natural sciences that can drive innovation and societal benefits worldwide. It provides detailed data on research growth, especially in China, reflecting meaningful changes in scientific leadership and capacity with potential large-scale impact.
articles.personality_title: Beijing leads global cities in high-quality science research in 2025
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Over the past decade, cities around the world have been competing to produce high-quality scientific research. The Nature Index tracks this progress by measuring how much top research each city contributes in natural science fields like biology, chemistry, and earth sciences.

**What happened** – The latest data for 2025 shows Beijing remains the top city globally for natural science research. Five other Chinese cities joined the top ten, showing strong growth in science output. Meanwhile, two US cities that were once in the top 10 dropped out of the top 20. In biology, the top 10 cities are more spread out, including four from China, four from the US, and two from Europe. In chemistry, Chinese cities took all top ten spots, with Beijing and Shanghai nearly doubling their research shares. For earth and environmental sciences, Beijing contributed 25% of China’s total research share, with Qingdao showing the fastest growth.

**Impact** – This shift highlights China’s growing strength and leadership in scientific research across multiple fields. It also shows how cities can rapidly increase their research quality and output, which may encourage more collaboration and innovation worldwide. The diverse mix in biology research suggests some areas still have broad international competition.

**What's next step** – Cities that are rising in these rankings may attract more funding, talent, and partnerships to further boost their research. Countries might invest more in science to stay competitive. Tracking these changes over time will help understand how global science leadership evolves.

**One-sentence takeaway** – In 2025, Beijing leads a growing group of Chinese cities dominating high-quality natural science research, reshaping the global scientific landscape.
articles.personality_title_fr: Pékin en tête des villes mondiales pour la recherche scientifique de haute qualité en 2025

articles.personality_title_es: Pekín lidera las ciudades globales en investigación científica de alta calidad en 2025
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante la última década, las ciudades del mundo han competido para producir investigaciones científicas de alta calidad. El Índice Nature mide estos avances contando cuánto aporta cada ciudad a investigaciones importantes en ciencias naturales como biología, química y ciencias de la Tierra.

**Qué pasó** – Los datos más recientes de 2025 muestran que Pekín sigue siendo la ciudad líder mundial en investigación en ciencias naturales. Cinco ciudades chinas más entraron en el top 10, mostrando un fuerte crecimiento. Dos ciudades de Estados Unidos que antes estaban en el top 10 cayeron fuera del top 20. En biología, el top 10 es más diverso, con cuatro ciudades chinas, cuatro estadounidenses y dos europeas. En química, las ciudades chinas ocuparon los diez primeros puestos, con Pekín y Shanghái casi duplicando su participación. En ciencias de la Tierra y medio ambiente, Pekín aportó el 25 % de la participación total de China, y Qingdao tuvo el mayor crecimiento.

**Impacto** – Este cambio destaca el creciente liderazgo de China en la investigación científica en varios campos. También muestra cómo las ciudades pueden aumentar rápidamente la calidad y cantidad de su investigación, lo que puede impulsar más innovación y colaboración global. La diversidad en biología indica que algunos campos siguen siendo muy competitivos.

**Próximo paso** – Las ciudades en ascenso podrían atraer más fondos, talento y asociaciones para fortalecer su investigación. Los países podrían invertir más para mantenerse competitivos. Seguir estos cambios ayudará a entender cómo evoluciona el liderazgo científico mundial.

**Resumen en una frase** – En 2025, Pekín lidera un grupo creciente de ciudades chinas que dominan la investigación científica de alta calidad, cambiando el panorama científico global.
